opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me again, it's always fun to be back.

I think 2026 is going to be less about the raw pre-training scale race and more about what you do *after* pre-training. If you look at what happened over the last year or so, a lot of the most interesting gains came from the post-training side: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, better reasoning training, and inference-time scaling, where you let the model "think" longer or sample multiple candidate answers and pick the best one. I expect companies to keep pushing hard there, because the returns are still pretty good compared to just throwing more data and compute at pre-training.

Related to that, I think a big focus will be efficiency. Reasoning models are great, but they're expensive to run because they generate so many tokens. So there's a lot of pressure to make them smarter about *when* to think long and when to just answer. You'll see more work on adaptive reasoning budgets, distillation of reasoning behavior into smaller models, and architectural tweaks: mixture-of-experts, more efficient attention variants, hybrid architectures that mix in linear attention or state-space-style layers to handle long contexts more cheaply. None of these individually is revolutionary, but together they add up.

The other area I'd point to is tool use and agentic workflows. Benchmarks are kind of saturated at this point, so the differentiator becomes how reliably a model can actually do multi-step tasks: calling tools, writing and running code, recovering from errors. That's where a lot of practical value is, and it's also where training is still pretty immature. Getting good reward signals for long-horizon tasks is hard, so I think there will be a lot of effort on environments and evaluation for that.

And finally, on the more applied side, I think many companies will invest less in building their own foundation models and more in specialization: taking strong open-weight models and fine-tuning or adapting them for their domain, with their own data. The open-weight models have gotten really good, so for a lot of organizations the question is no longer "can we build a frontier model," it's "how do we make a capable model work reliably for *our* problem." That's honestly where I'd put my money if I were a company that's not one of the big labs.

r001.rationale: The response predicts continued investment in reasoning training and adaptive reasoning, describing these as areas companies will keep pushing in 2026.

r002.rationale: It explicitly expects companies to keep pushing inference-time scaling, including letting models think longer or sample multiple answers.

r003.rationale: It identifies tool use and agentic workflows as a major focus, emphasizing reliable multi-step tasks, tool calls, code execution, and error recovery.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I'd break it into a few buckets, because I think "innovation" means pretty different things depending on who you are.

For the frontier labs, I expect the focus to stay on reasoning and inference-time scaling. The pretraining side hasn't disappeared, but the big leaps we've seen recently came from reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and from letting models spend more tokens thinking. There's still a lot of headroom there, but also a lot of open questions: how do you make reasoning efficient instead of just verbose, how do you get it to generalize beyond math and code where the reward signal is clean, and how do you keep the models from overthinking simple problems. I think adaptive compute, where the model decides how hard a problem is before it starts, is going to be a real theme.

For most companies, though, the innovation isn't going to be in training foundation models. It's going to be in agents, tool use, and the plumbing around them. The models are good enough now that the bottleneck is less about raw capability and more about reliability over long horizons. Can the system run for twenty steps without drifting off? Can it recover from a bad tool call? Can you evaluate it? I think a lot of engineering effort in 2026 goes into evaluation harnesses and into things that sound boring but matter, like memory, context management, and verification layers.

The third bucket is efficiency and small models. I keep coming back to this because I think it's underrated. Mixture-of-experts, distillation from larger reasoning models, quantization-aware training, the architectural tweaks around attention like sliding windows or latent attention. A lot of that is making models that run locally or at a fraction of the cost genuinely competitive for narrow tasks. And companies care about cost once they move past the demo phase.

And then one thing I'd flag that's more of a hope than a prediction: I'd like to see more focus on open weights and reproducible research. The open models coming out of China really pressured everyone last year, and I think that competition is healthy. Whether the Western labs respond by opening up more, or by pulling back, is going to shape what the research community can actually build on.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that frontier labs will continue focusing on reasoning in 2026, citing further headroom and open questions.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts continued focus on inference-time scaling, including letting models spend more tokens thinking.

r003.rationale: It predicts that most companies will focus on agents and tool use, emphasizing reliability over long horizons and systems running through many steps.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the focus will be on making these models more useful for specific tasks. There’s still room to improve the underlying models, of course, but for a company, the question is really: Can we make this work reliably on our data, in our workflow, at a cost that makes sense?

So I would expect more work on smaller, specialized models, better retrieval, and fine-tuning where it actually helps. You don’t necessarily need the largest model for every step of a system. Sometimes a smaller model that does one thing well is a better fit.

And then there’s evaluation. If you’re building an agent that takes several steps, you need to know whether it completes the task correctly, not just whether its responses sound good. I think a lot of the meaningful innovation will be in that whole system around the model—how you give it context, what tools it can use, and how you check its work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task-specific models and system reliability, but does not predict that improving LLM reasoning will remain a major innovation focus.

r002.rationale: It mentions cost and smaller models, but does not predict inference scaling as a major focus.

r003.rationale: It predicts innovation in the system around the model and specifically discusses multi-step agents, their tools, and checking whether they complete tasks correctly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the focus will be on making these models useful for specific business problems. Rather than training a large model from scratch, most companies will probably start with an existing model and figure out how to adapt it to their data and workflows.

And that’s more than just fine-tuning. It’s deciding what information the model needs, what tools it can access, and how you evaluate whether it actually does the job reliably. I expect more interest in smaller models, too, especially when companies can get the performance they need at a lower cost.

So, for me, the interesting question is how much value you can get out of a model in a particular application. Can you make it reliable enough, efficient enough, and easy enough to use that people actually benefit from it? I think that’s where a lot of the innovation will happen.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting models to business problems and making them reliable, but does not predict that improving LLM reasoning will remain a major innovation focus.

r002.rationale: It mentions efficiency and smaller models, but does not predict inference scaling as a major focus.

r003.rationale: It mentions tool access, but does not predict optimizing agentic systems that run LLMs in loops.
